endorsements.quote: Good model performance can be assured only through testing on data acquired from a range of real-world settings55, which are truly representative of the settings of intended use, and this is reflected by the VTPS (Table 1).

Notwithstanding efforts to validate AI tools before approval, unintended generalisation, shortcut learning54, biases in the function of the algorithm56, and other errors in performance often become apparent only when the MDSW is used in the real world for its intended indication but in an unselected population.
We propose that the total score (with possible values from 4 to 12) should be linked to requirements for clinical evaluation before and after an AI tool is approved.

unlisted_practices: Regulators should require prospective clinical investigations in the appropriate phases of AI medical device software evaluation, even where retrospective data are used for initial training, testing and validation.
Manufacturers should score the most critical possible use of an AI tool when determining its risk, to account for off-label drift.
Regulators should not classify an AI tool as low-risk solely because a human-in-the-loop is planned to verify its output.
Regulators should allow lower-risk AI tools with favourable benefit-risk to reach market with graded pre-market evidence balanced by formal post-market follow-up.
Regulators should apply stricter regulatory follow-up to withdraw AI medical device software when post-release evidence shows a negative benefit-risk ratio.
Healthcare professionals should disclose AI use to patients, including benefits, disadvantages, explainability, evidence, alternatives, and consequences of non-use.
Manufacturers and regulators should make transparent to end-users whether an AI tool is explainable and how rigorously it was validated and tested.
Developers should inform users of limited evidence for subpopulations or minority groups when a tool is not powered for them.
Post-release surveillance should notify end-users when they use the AI tool outside its validated indication and context.
Regulators should require extended pre-market clinical evaluation when the clinical performance score is 5 or more, or the sum of clinical performance and technical performance scores is 6 or more.
Manufacturers should not allow human oversight to shift responsibility and accountability for AI outputs solely from the manufacturer to the supervising human.

screen.reason: This is a framework/proposal by the CORE-MD consortium outlining a risk score for regulatory evaluation and governance of AI-based medical devices.
